newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, NATO face more work on pact after agreement.
newsitem.headline: Russia, NATO face more work on pact after agreement.

text.p: Leaders of the NATO western alliance and Russia must put the smiles of relief that greeted their long-awaited accord behind them and face up on Thursday to the challenge of selling the deal back home.

The very fact that Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov and NATO Secretary General Javier Solana struck a deal in Moscow on Wednesday to chart relations between the old Cold War adversaries into a friendlier 21st century was a victory.

Russian President Boris Yeltsin, facing nationalist critics who see NATO plans to expand into eastern Europe as a result of his dismantling of the Soviet superpower, had compared tense negotiations last week to the Cuban missile crisis of 1962.
A clearly relieved Primakov said the deal was a "victory for reason" and U.S. President Bill Clinton called it an "historic step closer to a peaceful, undivided, democratic Europe".

But details of the accord, which must be approved by NATO's 16 member governments before leaders meet for a planned May 27 signing ceremony in Paris, indicated considerable room for interpretation, suggesting some sticking points may have been simply glossed over rather than removed altogether.

Addressing a domestic audience in a rare television interview on Wednesday, Yeltsin sounded as if Russia had won all the concessions it sought, including the right to block NATO decisions through a permanent joint Russia-NATO council.

"Decisions can be taken only by consensus. If Russia is against some decision, it means this decision will not go through," Yeltsin said. The deal eased Russia's fears, he said, that NATO's plan to admit former Soviet-bloc states would threaten its security and create a new divisions in Europe.
But Clinton, who has insisted NATO will not treat new members like Poland and Hungary as "second-class citizens", was adamant Russia would have no veto over alliance decisions.
"Russia will work closely with NATO but not in NATO, giving Russia a voice but not a veto over NATO's business," he said.
Such apparent differences of opinion over the working of the the council, the central plank of the NATO-Russia Founding Act, suggest both sides still have some explaining to do.
Yeltsin also said the treaty would be binding on its signatories, even though it will not, as Russia had initially wanted, be ratified by national parliaments.

He indicated that such binding commitments would, in his view, oblige NATO not to deploy its forces or nuclear weapons on the territory of new member states or to store arms there or use former Warsaw Pact military installations.
But while NATO restated its commitment not to place nuclear arms or foreign troops in new territories, it did not renounce its right to do so.

The alliance also offered not to use the military facilities of the Warsaw Pact but insisted any country had the right to upgrade military installations as it felt fit. The Act restates the right of states to choose their own security arrangements.
Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are favourites to be handed the first invitations to join the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation at a summit in Madrid in July.
Those countries will be seeking assurances membership will truly bring them the security they still crave after half a century of Soviet communist domination.
"The agreement should not create a second-class membership category and must in no way provide for delaying the alliance's expansion," Polish Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati said.
Yeltsin, anxious to maintain good relations with the West, acknowledged he was making the best of an unwanted situation.
"We are against expansion," he told Russian Television.

"But considering the realities, both historic and, unfortunately, in real life, it has gone too far and we have to deal with this and minimise the risk for Russia or even remove it altogether...That's what this document aims to do."
